edge_138.evidence_note: Comparative teaching link, not an assertion of a one-way genealogy or agreement between Bloor and Latour. Compare sociological explanation and laboratory ethnography; shared objects do not establish a simple Bloor-to-Latour lineage. Latour’s Pasteur book explicitly questions explanation by the social alone; preserve this disagreement. The 1999 exchange now supplies a concrete disagreement: Bloor defends material and social causal explanation; Latour contests the assigned roles of objects and society. A separate contribution records his explicit earlier debt without implying continued agreement.

science.label: History of science
science.date_label: Earlier roots · History of Science Society founded 1924 · later approaches
science.description: Studies scientific knowledge, practices, instruments, institutions, and their historical settings. Histories of ideas, social and cultural histories, and material approaches coexist. The field predates Kuhn and STS, which transform parts of its questions without founding or exhausting it.
science.representative_figures_and_works: George Sarton; Alexandre Koyré, Études galiléennes (1939); Robert K. Merton; Thomas Kuhn, The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962); Steven Shapin and Simon Schaffer, Leviathan and the Air-Pump (1985). Yates and Foucault provide additional, distinct contributions; they do not substitute for these historians and programmes. Further approaches include Metzger’s history of chemistry (1923), Maier’s medieval natural philosophy (1949), Fleck’s scientific fact (1935), Needham’s collaborative Chinese science project (from 1954), Rossiter’s Women Scientists in America (1982), and Merchant’s The Death of Nature (1980).

science.scope_note: Kuhn is a central reorientation, not the field’s sole founder. Sarton, Koyré, Merton, and historians of experimental practice distinguish important approaches; Yates and Foucault are additional contributions. Chinese science and women’s scientific work expand this selection; it still needs fuller coverage of other regions and material practices. Named Chinese-series contributors and Daston/Galison’s image and instrument studies deepen the selection. Publication credits do not replace primary argument checks; wider regional coverage remains selective. Arabic mathematics, colonial Indian science, African healing and a Beninese knowledge programme are separate selected projects, not regional proxies or exhaustive coverage.

ssk.label: Sociology of scientific knowledge / SSK
ssk.description: Investigates how scientific beliefs become accepted within social practices and institutions. The Edinburgh Strong Programme seeks causal explanations of both accepted and rejected knowledge using the same kinds of explanation. SSK includes different programmes; it is neither all sociology of science nor all STS. Collins’s replication studies and Pinch’s work on controversies expose additional empirical programmes; these differ from treating SSK as only Bloor’s principles. Bloor explicitly includes material causes and rejects equating symmetry with equal credibility. His disagreement with Latour concerns the analytical roles of objects and society.
ssk.representative_figures_and_works: David Bloor, Knowledge and Social Imagery (1976; second edition 1991); Barry Barnes. The symmetry principle is a rule for explanation, not a claim that all scientific assertions have equal evidential merit. Barnes, Bloor and Henry, Scientific Knowledge (1996); Collins, Changing Order (1985); Pinch and Bijker, “The Social Construction of Facts and Artefacts” (1984).

consumption.label: Consumption & material culture
consumption.description: Examines commercial promotion, household demand, goods’ changing value, taste, gender and provisioning. McKendrick, Brewer and Plumb distinguish commercial and social changes; de Vries connects consumption with household labor; Mintz links diets to colonial production. Anthropological and feminist approaches ask how objects acquire meanings and how consumer roles depend on unequal social relations.

Additional readings: Douglas and Isherwood, The World of Goods (1979); Kopytoff on cultural biography (1986); de Vries on industrious change (1994); de Grazia and Furlough, The Sex of Things (1996). Maxine Berg and Helen Clifford, eds.: Consumers and Luxury (1999).

consumption.scope_note: Demand, taste, provisioning, commodities, and material objects are not one theory; gender and empire connect consumption to production. Commodity circulation, cultural biography and goods as communication are distinct questions. De Vries acknowledges conflicting household interests; feminist research does not reduce women to consumers. Much of this selection concerns Europe and the United States; Mintz’s colonial production connects regions but does not make the coverage global in every respect.

strands.title: Purchasing as household work
strands.focus: Vickery’s selected households distribute purchasing tasks and authority unevenly. Expenditure diaries show practical expertise, but incomplete income records limit reconstruction of financial power.

strands.title: Material meanings and unequal possibilities
strands.focus: Vickery finds social ambition alongside attachment and remembrance. Age, resources and inheritance matter; her chapter does not establish one feminine attitude to possessions.

strands.title: Competing chronologies and questions
strands.focus: Compare McKendrick’s eighteenth-century acceleration, Weatherill’s earlier middling ownership and de Vries’s household labor argument. Vickery questions universal motives. Different evidence and outcomes do not yield one automatic date for a consumer society.

strands.title: Ming consumers and social distinctions
strands.focus: Clunas reads Wen Zhenheng’s judgments about appropriate objects as elite distinctions, then compares them with Yan Song’s confiscation inventory. These are different sources, not interchangeable records of actual purchasing.

strands.title: Whose consumption becomes visible?
strands.focus: Clunas’s selected texts privilege elite men. Rules assigning objects to women do not directly recover women’s own meanings; subsistence consumers also remain poorly represented. Pagani highlights this limit while praising the method.

strands.title: Relics and changing value
strands.focus: Geary follows transfers and renewed authentication of relics. Their careers may change how communities value them; price equivalences and the relative frequency of different transfers remain uncertain.

strands.title: Specific historical uses of theory
strands.focus: Vickery explicitly uses Bourdieu and Douglas/Isherwood; Geary cites Kopytoff. These establish particular uses with different evidence and questions, without proving uniform reception across consumption history.

strands.title: Luxury and European consumer culture
strands.focus: Berg and Clifford coedit a volume on luxury and consumer culture in Europe, 1650–1850. This records their editorial contribution; detailed chapter arguments remain unchecked.
